title: 10 Best UX Design Websites to Learn From in 2026
description: The ten UI/UX design websites worth your time, every link opened and verified in October 2026, with what each one is free for and what it charges.

blocks.v: There is no shortage of lists like this one. The problem with most of them is that nobody checks the links afterwards, so you work through ten recommendations and find three dead domains, two sites that have quietly become something else, and a paywall where the free course used to be.

Every site below was opened and read on 1 October 2026 before it was listed. Where a site has changed since this article was first published, the entry says so. Where something is free, it says what is free and what is not, because "free resource" usually means a free article and a paid course.
These are the ten worth your time, roughly in the order a working designer would actually use them.
How to use this list
Reading design websites is not the same as learning design, and it is worth being honest about which one you are doing. Most people who bookmark twenty UX blogs end up reading none of them.

A better approach is to pick one site for each of three jobs. One for research you can cite when somebody questions a decision. One for a structured course if you are learning from scratch. One for a weekly habit, so you see what the field is arguing about. Everything else is reference material you search when a specific problem lands on your desk.
Each entry below says which of those three jobs it does.
1. Nielsen Norman Group

If you only use one site on this list, use this one. Nielsen Norman Group was founded by Jakob Nielsen and Don Norman, and it is the closest thing user experience has to a standards body. When you need to tell a client that their idea will not work, this is where the evidence comes from. The articles are research-backed rather than opinion, which matters enormously in a field where most advice is somebody's preference stated confidently.

v: Best for: settling arguments with evidence
Free: a very large archive of articles, plus a YouTube channel with short research summaries
Paid: training courses and UX certification, priced for companies rather than individuals
Start with: their articles on usability heuristics, which underpin most of the field

blocks.v: 2. Interaction Design Foundation

The largest structured UX education platform online, and the one to use if you want a course rather than a blog. The teaching is organised into proper courses with a beginning and an end, which is exactly what most self-taught designers are missing. It is worth knowing the model before you sign up: the courses run on an annual membership rather than per-course pricing.

v: Best for: learning in a structured order instead of reading at random
Free: a large encyclopedia of UX literature and their design blog
Paid: membership, which unlocks the courses and certificates
Start with: the free encyclopedia chapters before you decide whether to pay

blocks.v: 3. UX Collective

A community publication where working designers write about what they are actually running into. Because it publishes many authors rather than one house voice, the quality varies, but the range is the point: you get accessibility, research methods, design critique and career writing in the same feed. Their newsletter is one of the few in this field worth keeping subscribed to.

v: Best for: a weekly habit, and seeing what practitioners are arguing about
Free: most articles
Note: it is published on Medium, so some articles sit behind Medium's paywall
Start with: the newsletter rather than the site, so it comes to you

blocks.v: 4. Growth.Design

Case studies presented as comics, which sounds gimmicky and is not. Each one walks through a real product decision made by a company you have heard of, then explains the psychology behind why it worked or failed. If you have ever struggled to explain to a client why a change matters, this is the site that teaches you how to tell that story.

v: Best for: understanding the psychology under an interface, and learning to explain it
Free: the case studies
Paid: their courses and premium material
Start with: any case study on a product you already use, so you can check their reasoning against your own experience

blocks.v: 5. Untools

Not a design site at all, which is why it is on the list. Untools is a collection of thinking tools and decision-making frameworks: first principles, second-order thinking, systems maps, and similar. Design problems are usually thinking problems wearing a visual disguise, and this is the site that gives you a structure for the thinking part. Small, free, and completely free of filler.

v: Best for: untangling a problem before you open a design tool
Free: all of it
Start with: the decision-making section

blocks.v: 6. Laws of UX

A single-purpose reference site collecting the psychological principles that come up constantly in interface work: Hick's Law, Fitts's Law, Jakob's Law, the Von Restorff effect, and the rest. Each one gets a plain explanation and the research behind it. This was not in the original version of this article and should have been, because it is the fastest way to put a name to something you already do instinctively.

v: Best for: naming the principle behind a decision you have already made
Free: all of it
Start with: Jakob's Law, which explains most arguments about "making it look different"

blocks.v: 7. Baymard Institute

The most specific site here, and the most valuable if you work on anything that takes payment. Baymard runs large-scale usability research on e-commerce and publishes the findings, including a long-running benchmark of checkout usability across major retailers. If you are designing a cart, a checkout or a product page, this is research you can hand a client directly.

v: Best for: e-commerce, checkout and anything with a conversion target
Free: a substantial portion of their research articles
Paid: full research access and their benchmark database
Start with: their checkout usability findings

blocks.v: 8. UX Hints

Short, specific posts on one idea at a time, organised by topic: accessibility, typography, usability, user testing, UX laws. It still runs the "UX Hints TL;DR" format the name is known for. Useful when you have a narrow question and do not want a 3,000-word essay around the answer.

v: Best for: a quick answer to a specific question
Free: the articles and the newsletter
Start with: the topic index rather than the homepage

blocks.v: 9. Usability Geek

A long-running usability and UX blog with a practical bent. Where Nielsen Norman Group writes the research, Usability Geek tends to write the version you can apply on Monday morning. Strong on accessibility and on the unglamorous parts of usability that get skipped.

v: Best for: practical usability writing you can act on immediately
Free: the blog
Paid: they also list UX courses
Start with: their accessibility writing

blocks.v: 10. Dark Patterns Tip Line

A public archive of deceptive design: the countdown timers that reset, the unsubscribe buttons hidden three screens deep, the pre-ticked boxes. It exists so people can report what has been done to them, which makes it a catalogue of exactly the techniques you should refuse to build. Read it as a list of things to say no to when somebody asks for "something that converts better".

v: Best for: recognising a manipulative pattern before you are asked to build one
Free: all of it
Related: Ethical Design Resources at ethicaldesignresources.com collects the positive version, which is a curated set of tools and references for designing responsibly

blocks.v: One correction from the earlier version of this article

The original list included a site called "Principle.Design" and described it as a prototyping tool for building animated app interfaces. That conflated two different things, and it is worth correcting rather than quietly deleting.

Principle is a Mac prototyping application. principles.design is something else entirely: a free library of real-world design principles published by actual companies and teams, collected as decision-making frameworks. It is a genuinely useful site, it is simply not a prototyping tool. If you were looking for the prototyping application, that is a separate product. If you want the principles library, it is worth a visit for a different reason: reading how other teams wrote their principles is the fastest way to write your own.
Also worth bookmarking
Three more that did not make the ten but earn a place in a browser folder.
Smashing Magazine
Long-form, technically detailed articles sitting at the join between design and front-end code. Particularly good when the problem is a design decision with engineering consequences.
Ethical Design Resources
A curated, maintained collection of tools and references for designing responsibly. Small and still actively updated.
Nielsen Norman Group on YouTube
Listed separately from the main site because the format changes how useful it is. Short videos, usually one research finding each, and easier to get through than the written archive.
If you are starting from zero

Pick three, not ten. A reasonable starting set is Interaction Design Foundation for structure, Nielsen Norman Group for evidence, and the UX Collective newsletter for a weekly pulse. That covers learning, proving and keeping up.

Then build something. Every site on this list is more useful once you have a real interface in front of you and a specific problem to solve. Reading about usability heuristics in the abstract is far less effective than reading them while looking at a screen you designed and cannot work out why people are abandoning.
Frequently asked questions
What is the difference between UI and UX design?

UX is the decision about what the product does and in what order. UI is the decision about how that looks and behaves on screen. A booking flow that asks for payment before showing the price is a UX problem, and no amount of visual polish fixes it. A booking flow with the right steps but unreadable text is a UI problem. In practice one person often does both, but they fail in different ways and it helps to know which one you are looking at.
Which of these websites is best for a complete beginner?

Interaction Design Foundation, because it is organised as courses rather than as a feed. Beginners usually suffer from too much unordered information rather than too little, and a structured sequence solves that. Laws of UX is a good second, because it gives you vocabulary quickly.
Are any of these actually free?

Untools, Laws of UX and Dark Patterns Tip Line are entirely free. Nielsen Norman Group, Growth.Design, Baymard and Interaction Design Foundation publish a substantial amount free and charge for courses, certification or full research access. UX Collective is free except where an article sits behind Medium's paywall.
What are dark patterns?

Interface designs that work against the person using them: a cancel button hidden behind four screens, a pre-ticked subscription box, a countdown that resets when you reload. They are called deceptive design patterns in current regulatory language. They often do raise short-term conversion, which is why clients ask for them, and they damage trust and increasingly attract regulatory attention. The Dark Patterns Tip Line is a catalogue of them.
Do I need a design degree to work in UI/UX?

No. Portfolios decide hiring in this field, not qualifications. What a portfolio has to show is reasoning rather than screenshots: what the problem was, what you tried, what the result was. Three projects explained properly will beat twenty pretty images. Every site on this list helps you build the reasoning half.
How often should I be reading these?

One newsletter weekly, and the rest on demand when a specific problem arrives. Trying to read all ten regularly is how people end up reading none of them. Reference sites are for searching, not for subscribing.
Last checked and updated on 1 October 2026. Every link above was opened and verified on that date.

title: UX vs UI The Perfect Balance for a Winning Product

blocks.v: UX vs. UI: The Perfect Balance for a Winning Product
Introduction

In the world of digital design, two terms often come up—User Experience (UX) and User Interface (UI). While they are closely related, they serve distinct purposes. UX focuses on the overall feel of a product, ensuring it meets user needs efficiently, while UI is responsible for the look, feel, and interactive elements that enhance usability.

Understanding the synergy between UX and UI is crucial for creating successful products. Without UX, you risk designing something that doesn’t solve real user problems. Without UI, even the best ideas can feel confusing or unpolished. Let’s dive deeper into how UX and UI work together and why they’re essential.
UX is the Guide

User Experience (UX) design is all about creating a seamless, intuitive experience for users. It involves research, wireframing, user testing, and iterative design to make sure the product meets user needs efficiently.

v: UX helps uncover what users truly need.
It ensures products solve real-world problems.
A strong UX strategy leads to better engagement and conversions.
Without UX, you’re just making assumptions about user behavior.

blocks.v: UI is the Craft
User Interface (UI) design focuses on the visual elements and interactive components of a product. It ensures that users not only understand how to navigate but also enjoy the process.

v: UI enhances usability with clean, intuitive design.
It makes digital experiences aesthetically pleasing.
A well-crafted UI boosts user engagement and retention.
Without UI, even the best ideas can feel clunky or outdated.

blocks.v: Together, They Create Magic
UX and UI are not competitors—they complement each other to build user-friendly, engaging digital products. Here’s how they work together:

v: UX finds the right problem to solve, UI brings it to life.
A strong UX ensures users find what they need effortlessly.
UI makes the journey smooth, intuitive, and visually appealing.
UX is about logic and flow; UI is about aesthetics and interaction.
Without UX, UI is just decoration. Without UI, UX feels incomplete.
A great UX keeps users engaged; a refined UI makes them stay.
UX is the blueprint; UI is the final masterpiece.
When UX and UI align, products become unforgettable.

blocks.v: Why Businesses Must Invest in UX & UI
Investing in UX and UI isn’t just about making things look good—it directly impacts business success. Companies that prioritize UX/UI design experience:

v: Higher conversion rates – A smooth, engaging experience encourages users to take action.
Better customer satisfaction – Users appreciate seamless interactions and intuitive design.
Stronger brand loyalty – A well-designed product keeps users coming back.
Reduced development costs – Catching usability issues early prevents costly redesigns.

blocks.v: Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)
1. What is the difference between UX and UI?

UX (User Experience) focuses on the functionality, usability, and overall experience of a product, while UI (User Interface) deals with the visual and interactive elements that make the product engaging and easy to use.
2. Why is UX/UI important for a business?
Good UX/UI design leads to better user engagement, higher conversion rates, and improved customer satisfaction, ultimately helping businesses grow and retain loyal customers.
3. Can a product succeed with just good UX or UI alone?

Not really. A product with great UX but poor UI may be functional but unappealing, while a product with stunning UI but poor UX may be difficult to use. The best products strike a balance between both.
4. How does UX research improve design?
UX research helps designers understand user behavior, pain points, and needs, leading to data-driven design decisions that enhance usability and user satisfaction.
5. How often should UX/UI be updated?
Regular updates are recommended based on user feedback, changing trends, and evolving business needs. Continuous improvement ensures a product stays relevant and user-friendly.
Conclusion

UX and UI are the backbone of successful digital products. While UX ensures functionality and problem-solving, UI enhances the experience with aesthetics and ease of use. When these two elements work together, they create an engaging and effective product that users love.

Whether you're designing a website, app, or digital platform, investing in both UX and UI is key to long-term success. If you need expert help in crafting a seamless UX/UI experience, let’s connect and bring your vision to life!

useState is a React Hook that allows you to add state to functional components. It enables you to manage dynamic values within your component, such as user inputs, toggles, counters, or any data that may change over time.
const [state, setState] = useState(initialValue);

2. useEffect() react hook

useEffect is a React Hook that lets you perform side effects in functional components. It’s a replacement for lifecycle methods like componentDidMount, componentDidUpdate, and componentWillUnmount in class components.
It runs after the render is committed to the DOM and can be used for a variety of purposes such as fetching data, subscribing to events, or manipulating the DOM.

title: What Are EM and REM Units?
description: CSS uses various units to define lengths, such as px (pixels), % (percentages), and relative units like em and rem. Unlike absolute units like pixels, EM and

v: EM (Relative to Parent Element): EM units are relative to the font size of the element's parent. For instance, if the font size of the parent is 16px and you set an element's font size to 2em , the resulting size will be 2 * 16px = 32px . The EM unit cascades, meaning its value is affected by the parent element’s computed font size.

REM (Relative to Root Element): REM, short for “Root EM,” is always relative to the font size of the root element ( <html> ). For example, if the root element’s font size is 16px , setting an element’s font size to 2rem will result in 2 * 16px = 32px , regardless of its parent element.

blocks.v: Key Differences Between EM and REM

v: Reference Point:

blocks.v: EM depends on the font size of its immediate parent element.

v: REM always references the root element’s font size.
Cascading Behavior:

blocks.v: EM values are influenced by their parent’s computed styles, which can result in compounding effects.

v: REM values remain consistent across the document, making them more predictable.
Use Cases:

blocks.v: EM is useful when you want sizes to adjust based on their context (e.g., within a specific container).

v: REM is ideal for creating a consistent design system where sizes scale uniformly.

blocks.v: Why Use Relative Units Instead of Pixels?
Using relative units like EM and REM provides several benefits:

v: Scalability: Relative units make it easier to create responsive designs that adapt to different screen sizes and resolutions.
Accessibility: Users with visual impairments often adjust their browser’s default font size. Relative units ensure your design scales proportionally without breaking.
Maintainability: By defining sizes relative to a single root value, you can change the entire site’s scale by updating the root font size.

blocks.v: Practical Examples
1. Using EM for Nested Elements
In this example, the child element’s font size is calculated based on its parent (.container), resulting in cascading effects.
Here, all sizes reference the root element’s font size, ensuring a consistent scale throughout the site, regardless of the parent element.
You can use both EM and REM strategically. For instance, you might use REM for typography to maintain consistency and EM for spacing within components for flexibility.
This approach ensures predictable typography while allowing component-specific adjustments.
Common Pitfalls to Avoid

v: Compounding with EM: Nesting multiple elements with EM can result in unintended scaling. Always test your designs to avoid unexpected sizes.

Inconsistent Root Font Sizes: If you use REM units but don’t set a consistent root font size in your CSS, the browser’s default value (often 16px ) will be used. Define a root font size for better control.
Mixing Pixels with Relative Units: Avoid mixing px with EM or REM in the same context. This can create inconsistencies, especially in responsive designs.

blocks.v: When to Use EM vs. REM

v: Use EM when:

blocks.v: You want element sizes to depend on their parent container.

v: Creating modular components where styles adapt to context.
Use REM when:

blocks.v: You want a consistent scale across your entire site.

v: Defining global typography and spacing.

blocks.v: Tips for Mastering EM and REM

v: Set a Base Font Size: Define a root font size in the <html> element, e.g., html { font-size: 16px; } . This provides a predictable starting point.

title: 7 Tips to Improve CTR (Click-Through Rate)
description: 7 tips to improve CTR (Click-Through Rate), a key digital marketing metric that measures how often people click on your link after seeing it in search results.

blocks.v: Click-through rate (CTR) is one of the most crucial metrics in digital marketing. It reflects how often people click on your link after seeing it in search results, emails, or ads. Improving your CTR is essential for driving traffic and achieving your marketing goals. Here are seven actionable tips to help you boost your CTR, each supported by best practices for search engine optimization (SEO).
1. Ensure Title Tags and H1 Work Together

Your title tag and H1 heading are the first impressions your content makes. While they don’t have to be identical, they should complement each other. The title tag appears in search results and should be optimized for clicks, while the H1 is the headline users see on the page itself.

v: Tip : Craft a title tag that grabs attention but remains relevant to the content.
Example : If your title tag is "10 Ways to Save on Travel," your H1 could be "Your Ultimate Guide to Travel Savings in 2023."
SEO Insight : Google values clarity. Misalignment between the title tag and H1 can confuse users and search engines, potentially reducing your rankings.

blocks.v: 2. Write Irresistible, Honest Headlines

Your headline is the hook that draws readers in. A compelling headline can significantly increase your CTR, but it must remain truthful. Misleading headlines (clickbait) might drive clicks initially but will hurt your credibility and SEO in the long run.

v: Tip : Use power words like "proven," "ultimate," or "essential" to spark curiosity and excitement.
Example : "The Ultimate Guide to Mastering Social Media in 2025."
SEO Insight : Honest headlines improve dwell time—the amount of time users spend on your site—which is a positive signal for search engines.

blocks.v: 3. Keep Titles Short and Visible

Your titles should be concise and display fully in search engine results. Google typically displays only the first 50-60 characters of a title tag. Anything longer might get truncated, potentially leaving out key information.

v: Tip : Stick to a title length of 55 characters or less.
Example : Instead of "How to Improve Your Website’s SEO and Boost Traffic," try "Boost Traffic with Better SEO Tips."
SEO Insight : A clear, concise title is easier to read and process, making users more likely to click.

blocks.v: 4. Match Content to Search Intent

Understanding and addressing the intent behind a user’s search query is key to improving CTR. Search intent can be informational (seeking knowledge), navigational (finding a specific site), or transactional (ready to make a purchase).

v: Tip : Research the search intent for your target keywords and tailor your content accordingly.
Example : If users search for "best running shoes 2025," they likely want product comparisons and reviews, not a general blog about running.
SEO Insight : Content that aligns with search intent not only improves CTR but also boosts engagement and conversions.

blocks.v: 5. Highlight Your Unique Selling Point
Standing out in a crowded digital space requires emphasizing what makes your content, product, or service unique. Your unique selling point (USP) should be clear in your title and meta description.

v: Tip : Use your title to showcase value. For instance, "Free Shipping on Handmade Jewelry" instantly tells users what they gain.
Example : "Eco-Friendly Sneakers – Sustainable Comfort for Runners."
SEO Insight : Highlighting your USP can attract niche audiences and improve your rankings for long-tail keywords.

blocks.v: 6. Go Bold with a Fresh Perspective
A fresh take on a familiar topic can make your content more appealing. Avoid clichéd headlines and explore angles that resonate with your target audience.

v: Tip : Incorporate trends, data, or personal insights to add a unique spin.
Example : Instead of "Tips for Remote Work," try "Why Remote Work Is the Future: Insights for 2025."
SEO Insight : Unique content is more likely to earn backlinks, which can enhance your authority and search rankings.

blocks.v: 7. Add Bonus Value in Brackets
Adding brackets to your title can increase clicks by up to 38%, according to studies. Brackets allow you to highlight extra value, such as "[Free Guide]" or "[2025 Update]."

v: Tip : Use brackets sparingly to avoid overloading your title.
Example : "7 Productivity Hacks for Entrepreneurs [Free Checklist]."
SEO Insight : Brackets not only grab attention but also set expectations, improving CTR and reducing bounce rates.

blocks.v: Final Thoughts

Improving CTR requires a blend of creativity, audience understanding, and SEO best practices. By implementing these seven tips, you can craft compelling headlines and content that resonate with users and search engines alike. Remember, the ultimate goal is to provide value and meet user needs, ensuring sustainable growth for your digital presence.
Ready to boost your CTR? Start experimenting with these strategies today, and watch your click-through rates soar!

IndexedDB is a low-level API for client-side storage of large amounts of structured data. It allows for complex querying and indexing, making it perfect for offline web apps and caching data.
9. Web File API
The File API enables web applications to interact with local files selected by the user. It’s often used for file uploads, previews, or editing files directly in the browser.

    console.log("Selected file:", file);
    // Logs the selected file object to the console. This includes file metadata like name, size, and type.
  }
</script>
10. Web Notification API
The Notification API allows web apps to send notifications to the user, even when the browser is minimized. It’s a great way to engage users with updates, reminders, or alerts.
11. Web Workers API
Web Workers enable running JavaScript code in the background, without blocking the main thread. This API is crucial for improving performance in applications that require heavy computations.
12. Web Mutation Observer API
The Mutation Observer API provides a way to watch for changes to the DOM. It’s a powerful tool for observing and responding to dynamic content updates.
13. Web Pointer Lock API
The Pointer Lock API is used for locking the mouse pointer to a specific element. It’s often employed in immersive web applications, such as first-person games or 3D simulations.
14. Web Battery Status API
The Battery Status API provides information about the device’s battery level and charging status. This API helps developers optimize app behavior based on battery usage.
15. Web Gamepad API
The Gamepad API enables support for game controllers, allowing developers to create immersive gaming experiences directly in the browser.
16. Web Device Orientation and Motion API
This API provides access to the device's accelerometer and gyroscope data. It’s commonly used for motion-based interactions, such as tilting a device to control a game.
17. Web Push API
The Push API enables web applications to receive push notifications from a server, even when the application is not active. It’s a great tool for re-engaging users with updates or promotions.
18. Web Payment Request API
The Payment Request API streamlines the checkout process by integrating payment options directly into the browser. It enhances the user experience and reduces friction during transactions.
Conclusion

JavaScript Web APIs offer developers endless possibilities to enhance the functionality and interactivity of their applications. By leveraging these APIs, you can create innovative, user-friendly web experiences.

blocks.v: Introduction

JavaScript is a powerful language for web development, but as projects grow, managing complex codebases can become challenging. Enter TypeScript, a superset of JavaScript designed to add static typing, improve readability, and reduce bugs. This guide provides a comprehensive introduction to TypeScript for JavaScript developers, covering essential concepts like type inference, type definitions, unions, generics, and structural typing.
What is TypeScript?

TypeScript is an open-source programming language developed by Microsoft. It builds on JavaScript by adding optional static typing, making it easier to catch errors during development rather than runtime. TypeScript code compiles to plain JavaScript, ensuring compatibility with any environment that supports JavaScript.

v: Type Safety: Helps prevent runtime errors by catching issues during compilation.
Better Tooling: Enhanced IntelliSense and autocompletion in IDEs.
Maintainability: Makes large codebases easier to manage and scale.
Backward Compatibility: Works seamlessly with existing JavaScript libraries and frameworks.

blocks.v: Type Inference

TypeScript features type inference, which means it can automatically determine the type of a variable based on its initial value. This reduces the need for explicit type annotations, making code cleaner and more concise.

let calories = 89; // TypeScript infers 'number'
let fruits = ["Banana", "Orange"]; // TypeScript infers 'string[]'
While inference simplifies code, you can still explicitly define types when needed, especially for function parameters or complex data structures.
Defining Types
TypeScript allows you to define types for variables, function parameters, and return values, improving code clarity.
Defining types ensures that the data passed to and returned from functions is predictable and consistent.
Unions
Union types allow a variable to hold more than one type of value. This is useful when dealing with data that can vary between a few specific types.

type FruitSize = "S"  | "M"  | "L"
let validSize: FruitSize = "M"
let invalidSize: FruitSize = "Medium"; // Syntax error: "Medium" is not assignable to type 'FruitSize'.
Unions provide flexibility while maintaining type safety.
Generics

Generics let you create reusable components that work with multiple types while maintaining type safety. They are particularly useful for creating type-safe data structures like arrays or custom utilities.
Here, the identity function works with any type (T), and the type is determined when the function is called.
Structural Types
TypeScript uses a structural typing system, meaning compatibility between types is determined by their structure rather than their explicit declarations.
For example, if two objects have the same shape, they are considered compatible.
This flexibility makes TypeScript highly intuitive and adaptable for real-world scenarios.
Conclusion

TypeScript is a game-changer for JavaScript developers, offering powerful tools to enhance code quality and maintainability. By understanding its key features like type inference, type definitions, unions, generics, and structural typing, you can write cleaner, more reliable code.

In this tutorial, you’ll learn about state management in React, understand how props work, and why using a state management library like Redux can simplify your code.
Understanding State and the useState Hook
State is an important concept in React because it helps keep track of data that changes over time. Let’s start by using the useState hook to manage state within functional components.
The useState hook is used to create and manage the state in a functional component. It returns two values:

v: The current state (initially set to a value of your choice)
A function to update that state

blocks.v: const [counter, setCounter] = useState(0);
In this app, we’ll create three buttons to:

v: Increment the counter
Decrement the counter
Reset the counter

blocks.v: Here’s how the buttons will work:

setCounter(counter + 1)}>Increment
 setCounter(counter - 1)}>Decrement
 setCounter(0)}>Reset
With each button click, the state will update, and the component will re-render with the new counter value.
Organizing the Counter Appp
Next, we’ll turn our counter logic into a React component for better organization.

v: Create the Counter Component : Inside a folder named counter , create a file called Counter.js .
Use the rafce shortcut to generate a functional component quickly.

blocks.v: What Are Props?
Props (short for properties) allow React components to communicate with each other by passing data from parent components to child components. In the example above:

v: We keep the counter state and functions in the parent component.
Then, we pass them down to the child Counter component using props.

blocks.v: Props are very useful for passing values like numbers, arrays, and even functions between components. However, as your app grows, this can become tricky.
Understanding Prop Drilling

When you pass props from a parent component down to deeply nested child components, you end up with a lot of code just passing data down the tree. This is called prop drilling. Prop drilling can make your code messy and hard to maintain, especially if you need to pass data through multiple layers of components.
Solving Prop Drilling with Redux
To avoid the mess of prop drilling, we can use a state management library called Redux. Redux helps manage the state of your entire application in a central store.

v: What is Redux? Redux allows you to store your app’s state in one place, and any component can access the state without needing to pass props.
Why Redux? It eliminates the need to pass props down multiple components (solving prop drilling).
It keeps your state in one organized place.
